section.title: Widows, Elders, and Church Order
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns to the practical ordering of the church as a family. Different ages are to be treated with familial respect; true widows are to be honored and cared for, while families bear first responsibility for their own; elders who lead well deserve double honor, yet are subject to fair discipline. The chapter shows the household of God caring justly and tenderly for its members.
section.thesis: The church is God's family, so it must honor and provide for the truly needy, uphold the duty of families to care for their own, and treat its leaders with both generous honor and impartial accountability.
section.frameNote: Five movements: treating each age as family; honoring true widows and the duty of relatives; the enrollment of widows; double honor and fair discipline for elders; and a solemn charge to Timothy on impartiality and purity.

verses.text: Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers,
older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.
Honor the {{chera|widows}} who are truly widows.
But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show {{eusebeo|godliness}} to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.
But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive.
Give these instructions to the believers, so that they will be above reproach.
If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, faithful to her husband,
and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work.
But refuse to enroll younger widows. For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry,
and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith.
At the same time they will also learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention.
So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander.
For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.
If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened, so that it can help the widows who are truly in need.
{{presbyteros|Elders}} who lead effectively are worthy of double {{time|honor}}, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.
For the {{graphe|Scripture}} says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.”
Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.
But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.
I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality.
Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.
Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later.
In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.

chera.gloss: A widow, a woman who has lost her husband. Paul distinguishes those who are truly widows, alone and in need, from those with family able to help. The care of widows reaches back to God's special concern for them in the law and prophets and continues in the early church.

eusebeo.gloss: To show godliness or reverence, here toward one's own family; the verb form of eusebeia, godliness. Caring for aging parents and relatives is not a lesser, worldly duty but an expression of true godliness, pleasing in the sight of God.

presbyteros.gloss: An elder. The same word means an older man, as in verse 1, and the church office of elder, as here in verse 17. In the office sense it names the leaders who govern and teach, worthy of double honor when they lead well, especially those who labor in preaching.

time.gloss: Honor, respect, and by extension the material support that honor carries. Double honor for hardworking elders includes both esteem and financial provision, as the two quoted Scriptures about the ox and the worker's wages make clear.

graphe.gloss: Scripture, a writing regarded as God's word. Strikingly, Paul introduces both a quotation from Deuteronomy and a saying of Jesus with the Scripture says, placing the words of Jesus alongside the Old Testament as authoritative Scripture.

basic.context: Paul tells Timothy to treat the church as a family: older men as fathers, younger women as sisters, and so on. He gives careful instructions on widows, honoring those truly alone while insisting families care for their own. He gives wise counsel about younger widows, then turns to elders: those who lead well deserve double honor, but accusations must be tested and persistent sin rebuked openly. He charges Timothy to be impartial and to keep himself pure.
basic.hermeneutics: This is mostly practical wisdom for ordering church life, and its principles carry over even where the specific arrangements were shaped by that culture. The abiding truths stand out: honor and provide for the truly needy, families must care for their own, and leaders deserve both generous support and impartial accountability.
basic.originalLanguages: A chera, widow, truly alone is to be honored, while relatives must eusebeo, show godliness, to their own. Presbyteros means both older man and elder; elders who lead well deserve double time, honor. Paul cites the graphe, Scripture, quoting both Moses and Jesus as authoritative.
basic.typology: God's care for the widow, woven through the law and prophets, points to Christ who has compassion on the helpless and to the church as His family that cares for its own. The elder who labors in the word serves under Christ the Chief Shepherd.
basic.christ: The elders who work hard at preaching and teaching serve Christ's flock, and their support rests on Jesus' own word that the worker is worthy of his wages. The charge is given before God and Christ Jesus, whose gaze governs how the church is to be led.
basic.god: God is deeply concerned for the vulnerable and is pleased when families honor their own. He is the one before whom Timothy is charged, watching over the church's fairness. Care for widows and honesty in leadership are matters that touch His own heart and honor.
basic.crossReferences: James 1 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows. Deuteronomy 25 and Luke 10 stand behind verse 18. Acts 6 shows the early church organizing to care for widows.
basic.oneStory: God has always defended the widow, the orphan, and the poor, and called His people to reflect His compassion. Here the church is ordered as a caring family under accountable leaders. It is part of God's long work of forming a people whose life together shows His justice and mercy, gathered under Christ the Shepherd.

context.literary:
The chapter is held together by one image, the household, and it is introduced in the first verses by a set of family names: father, brothers, mothers, sisters. After that the chapter moves through three pieces of church business. Verses 3 to 16 deal with widows, verses 17 to 25 deal with elders, and the end of the chapter closes with a solemn charge in verse 21 and an aside on Timothy's health in verse 23. The widow section has its own internal shape. Verses 3 to 8 set out who is truly a widow and who must care for her. Verses 9 to 15 describe the enrolled widow and the younger widow. Verse 16 returns to the opening principle of family responsibility, so that the section begins and ends with relatives who must act. This looks like a deliberate ring.

The elders section is also compact. Verse 17 gives the rule, verse 18 gives its scriptural ground, verse 19 gives protection against false accusation, verse 20 gives the opposite, public rebuke for those who persist, and verse 21 lays an oath over the whole. Honour and discipline are held in one hand. A church that pays well but cannot correct is as unbalanced as one that corrects but never supports.

The closing verses 22 to 25 look scattered, but the thread is judgment and what is hidden. Hasty ordination, the remark on wine, and the final two verses about sins and good works that come to light later are all about not judging too quickly, whether in choosing leaders or in assessing them. The advice about wine is a pastoral aside placed in the middle of this because Timothy's own care of his body is part of his fitness to serve. The final two verses balance each other: some sins and some good deeds are obvious at once, and others only later, so patience is needed both ways.
context.historical:
A widow in the first-century Mediterranean world was often in real peril. There was no state pension. A woman's support came through husband, father or son, and where those were gone she could be left with nothing. Israel's law had made the widow, the orphan and the foreigner the special charge of the community, Exodus 22:22 and Deuteronomy 10:18, and the prophets accused the nation when it failed them, Isaiah 1:17. The early church took up the duty at once. Acts 6:1 to 6 records a daily distribution of food to widows in Jerusalem, a dispute over fairness in it, and the appointment of seven men to see it done. Acts 9:39 shows widows in Joppa grieving for Dorcas, who had made them clothing.

By the time of this letter the church at Ephesus seems to have had a recognised list of widows. Paul sets a standard: age sixty or more, a faithful marriage behind her, and a record of good works, hospitality, care of children and of the afflicted. The age and the record suggest that an enrolled widow was supported by the church and in return gave herself to prayer and to acts of mercy, much as Anna in Luke 2:37 gave her life to worship in the temple.

Honouring parents was a basic duty for Jews, Exodus 20:12. Jesus had rebuked the practice of declaring goods 'Corban,' given to God, in order to avoid supporting a mother or father, Mark 7:10 to 13. Paul is on the same ground. The reference to elders in verse 17 reflects the pattern in Ephesus described in Acts 20:17 and 20:28, where elders were called overseers and told to shepherd the church. Paying a teacher was an accepted idea, as the sayings of Jesus and Paul show in Luke 10:7 and 1 Corinthians 9:14.
context.canonical:
The care of widows is one of the steadiest threads in the Bible. God is called 'a defender of the widows,' Psalm 68:5, the Law protects them, and the prophets condemn rulers who ignore them, Isaiah 1:23. Jesus commended a widow who gave all she had, Mark 12:41 to 44, raised the only son of a widow at Nain, Luke 7:11 to 15, and told a parable of a widow who kept asking a judge for justice, Luke 18:1 to 8. James 1:27 says the pure religion before God is to care for orphans and widows in their distress.

The ox of verse 18 comes from Deuteronomy 25:4, and Paul draws the same principle in 1 Corinthians 9:9 to 14, where he argues that those who preach the gospel should live from the gospel. The second saying, 'The worker is worthy of his wages,' matches words of Jesus in Luke 10:7 and a similar saying in Matthew 10:10. The rule that an accusation needs two or three witnesses comes from Deuteronomy 19:15 and is applied by Jesus in Matthew 18:16.

The pattern of elders is found elsewhere: Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5, James 5:14 and 1 Peter 5:1 to 4. Hebrews 13:17 adds that leaders keep watch over souls as those who must give an account, which parallels the solemn charge in verse 21. Paul's charge to treat the church as a family continues in the phrase 'household of God' from 1 Timothy 3:15, and in Galatians 6:10, which speaks of those who belong to the family of faith.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the church at Ephesus to see itself as a household and to be conducted like one. In a household the strong care for the weak, relatives do not pass off their duty, and no one is turned away from help without a reason. He also wanted the church's gifts to be wisely used. A list of supported widows is limited, so those with family are sent first to their family, and those who are enrolled must be those who really need it and who really serve.

The instructions on elders aim at two dangers. One is stinginess toward leaders who labour, and the other is leniency or injustice toward leaders who sin. Verse 19 shields them from casual slander, and verse 20 refuses to shield them from public rebuke. The charge in verse 21 closes the door on favouritism, because partiality would ruin both. Paul wanted Timothy to be a steady, unbought, patient judge of people, one who does not lay hands on anyone quickly and who understands that the final truth about a person sometimes arrives late.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this chapter is specific to an arrangement in one church, and it should be read with that in mind. The age of sixty, the enrolment of widows, and the particular advice to younger widows to marry and manage households reflect a society in which a young widow had few other means of support or protection. Paul gives them as wisdom for that setting, and it would be wrong to read them as a rule that every church must keep a roll at sixty or that every young widow must remarry.

What clearly carries across is the principle. Families must care for their own, and Paul says that failing to do so is a denial of the faith. The church must use its resources for those in real need. Leaders who labour in the word deserve generous support. Accusations must be tested, and sin must be addressed honestly. The advice about wine in verse 23 is plainly personal and medical and should not be turned into a general rule on drink, nor into a ban on medicine. It shows that Paul was concerned for Timothy's body and that godliness and sensible care go together.

debates.question: What is the 'enrolment' of widows in verses 9 to 10?

views.label: A support list for those in need
views.case: The passage begins with those who are truly alone and in need, verse 5, and ends by saying the church must not be burdened so that it can help the widows who are truly in need, verse 16. On this reading the roll is a register of those the church will support, with conditions of age and character so the limited funds go to those who need and deserve them.

views.label: A recognised order of service
views.case: The conditions, sixty years, good deeds, a record of hospitality, feet-washing and relief for the afflicted, read like a description of a ministry, and the reference to younger widows incurring judgment for setting aside 'their first faith' suggests a pledge. On this reading the enrolled widow was supported and also commissioned to a life of prayer and service.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many see no sharp division. A widow who was supported was also expected to give herself to prayer and good works, as Anna did in Luke 2:37, and a simple pledge to this life of devotion would explain why remarriage afterwards was a matter for judgment.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the church's help was to be careful and fair, focused on those truly in need, and that a widow's life was supposed to bear fruit in prayer and mercy.

debates.question: What is 'double honor' in verse 17?

views.label: Financial support
views.case: The next verse quotes the ox that is allowed to eat while it treads grain and the worker who is worthy of his wages, both about material provision. The word for honour can also mean a price or payment. On this view double honour means generous pay for elders who work hard at preaching and teaching.

views.label: Respect and honour
views.case: The word is used for honour throughout the letter, 1 Timothy 5:3 and 6:1, and Paul uses it of respect. On this view the honour is the double esteem owed to a leader and a worker.

views.label: Both respect and payment
views.case: Most readers combine the two, since honour toward a labourer includes providing for him, and the double may mean 'twice the ordinary,' or 'honour and wages,' or an ample amount.

debates.bearing: The ox and the wage are about provision, so the sentence at least includes material support. Churches are not asked to treat their teachers as hired hands, but as workers who deserve a living.

debates.question: Is Paul calling Luke's Gospel 'Scripture' in verse 18?

views.label: He quotes a saying of Jesus now written down
views.case: The words 'the worker is worthy of his wages' match the saying in Luke 10:7 closely. If Luke was written before this letter, Paul places a Gospel beside Deuteronomy under the one word 'Scripture.' Some think this is an early sign that the church was already recognising apostolic writings.

views.label: He quotes a proverbial or spoken saying of Jesus
views.case: Others hold that Paul draws on a saying of Jesus that was known in the churches by word of mouth, which Luke and Matthew each record. The word 'Scripture' then covers the ox and the introduction of the second quote, without needing to assume a written Gospel.

debates.bearing: Either way, Paul treats the words of Jesus as carrying the same weight as the Law. The principle for elders rests on God's own word, not on custom.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening instruction uses a verb that is unusual in the New Testament. 'Rebuke' in verse 1 is epiplesso, to strike at with words, and Paul says not to do this to an older man, but to appeal to him, parakaleo, the word for coming alongside to encourage. In verse 2 the phrase 'with absolute purity' uses hagneia, moral cleanness, and is specific to the younger women. The familial words cover the whole congregation, so every relationship is reframed.

In verse 3, the phrase translated 'truly widows' is ontos chera, and ontos means in reality. In verse 5 the widow is 'left all alone,' using a perfect participle of monoo, which describes a settled state: she has been made alone and remains so. Her hope is set on God and she continues 'night and day' in prayer, the same phrase used of Anna in Luke 2:37. In contrast, verse 6 speaks of one who 'lives for pleasure,' from spatalao, a word for self-indulgence used in James 5:5, and says she is dead while living.

Verse 4 says children or grandchildren should 'show godliness,' and the verb eusebeo is the verb form of the noun eusebeia, used throughout the letter. The idea that godliness begins at home is deliberate. In verse 8, 'provide for' is pronoeo, to think ahead for, a word Paul uses in Romans 12:17 and 2 Corinthians 8:21. The phrase 'his own household' is the word oikeios, belonging to the house. The offence is described as having 'denied the faith,' a stronger statement than neglect.

In verse 9 the phrase 'the wife of one man' is literally 'one man's woman,' and it mirrors the phrase 'husband of but one wife' that Paul used of overseers in 3:2. Both phrases point to faithfulness, not necessarily to a never-remarried status, and the exact meaning has been discussed since the early church.

In verse 17, the phrase 'who lead effectively' translates the verb proistemi, which means to stand before, to lead and to care for. It is used of the household in 3:4, and of those who preside in 1 Thessalonians 5:12. The word 'work hard' is kopiao, the same toil word used in 4:10. Honour in the phrase 'double honor' is time, which can also mean a price or value. In verse 21 'without bias' translates a word, prosklisis, that means leaning toward one side, and 'partiality' appears with it. Verse 22 says 'laying on of hands' and warns that hasty action means to 'share,' koinoneo, in the sins of others. In verse 23 the phrase 'stop drinking only water' is a present imperative, hydropoteo, and the Greek says it is for the sake of 'your stomach and your frequent ailments.'

typology.type: The widow, the orphan and the stranger as God's own concern
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told to leave gleanings for the widow and to let her share in the feasts, Deuteronomy 24:19 to 21 and 16:11, as a picture of God's care. In the church this becomes a visible household. Jesus Himself, from the cross, entrusted His mother to the beloved disciple, John 19:26 to 27, an act of care in His last hour. The pattern falls short whenever it becomes mere charity from a distance. The Lord gives a family, not just a portion, and the church is called to be a family that knows its widows by name.

typology.type: The ox and the labourer at the threshing floor
typology.fulfillment: The law of the ox, Deuteronomy 25:4, was given for the animal and was also read as a principle for people, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9:9 to 10. The worker who feeds the grain eats from it. In Christ the labourer is the one who preaches the gospel, and the Lord Himself prescribes that such workers should receive their living, 1 Corinthians 9:14. The type falls short if it suggests the work earns salvation. The labour of the elder is service to a flock bought by Christ's blood, Acts 20:28, and its wage is a provision and not a price.

The law of Deuteronomy 19:15 protected the accused from the word of a single accuser. Jesus applied it to the settling of disputes in the church, Matthew 18:16, and Paul applies it to elders. The pattern is fulfilled in the way Christ's own cause is established by witnesses, as John 8:17 and 1 John 5:7 to 9 recall. It is a rule of justice and mercy that holds back rumour. It falls short when two witnesses are mistaken for proof, because the point of the rule is to prompt a careful hearing, not to settle the verdict in advance.

study.christ:
The chapter reaches Christ first through the family language. Paul asks Timothy to treat older men as fathers and young men as brothers because the church is a household of God, and the family exists because Christ has made believers His brothers. Hebrews 2:11 says He is not ashamed to call them brothers. The mutual care that Paul describes is the household life of those who share one Father and one elder Brother.

It reaches Christ through the widow. Jesus noticed widows and was moved by them: at Nain He saw a mother who had lost her only son and, full of compassion, He raised him, Luke 7:11 to 15. He praised the widow who gave her two small coins, Mark 12:41 to 44, and He condemned those who devoured widows' houses, Mark 12:40. On the cross He did what verse 8 requires of a son. He saw His own mother and gave her into the care of the disciple whom He loved, John 19:26 to 27. The demand that a family provide for its own is not only a rule but a picture of what Jesus did in the last hour of His life.

It reaches Christ through the elders who work hard at preaching and teaching. Peter calls Christ the Chief Shepherd and tells elders to shepherd the flock under Him, 1 Peter 5:1 to 4, and Paul tells the Ephesian elders to shepherd the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood, Acts 20:28. The elder's honour is real, but it is honour borrowed from the Shepherd whose sheep he feeds. The same Shepherd is the judge before whom both elders and flock stand.

The solemn charge in verse 21 places Timothy under the eye of 'God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels.' Paul's own words show Christ already ranked alongside the Father as the one before whom such oaths are sworn. Final judgment belongs to Him, which is why the end of the chapter looks forward to the time when what is hidden will be plain, verses 24 and 25. Paul elsewhere says the Lord will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and disclose the motives of the heart, 1 Corinthians 4:5.

A word of care: the passage does not make every widow a symbol or every ox a figure of Christ. The links above rest on the way Jesus and the apostles themselves speak. What the chapter offers is the way a Christ-shaped church orders its life, with tenderness for the needy, honour for faithful work, and honesty about sin.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the defender of those with no defender. Psalm 68:5 calls Him a father to the fatherless and a defender of widows, and the widow of verse 5 puts her hope in Him. Paul's instructions are what that character looks like when it is translated into the ordering of a congregation. A church that supports its widows is acting as God's hands.

It shows that God is pleased by ordinary duty. The sentence 'this is pleasing in the sight of God,' verse 4, applies to children who care for their parents, and nothing about it is dramatic. The God of this chapter is not impressed by religious display alone; He is pleased by a grandson who pays his grandmother's bills. To fail in this, Paul says, is to deny the faith. God takes domestic faithfulness seriously.

It shows God as just and unbiased. Timothy is charged to act without bias and without partiality, because God Himself shows none. The oath of verse 21 sets the whole of church discipline under a Judge who sees everything. This is also why the end of the chapter turns to hidden things: sins and good deeds that are not yet visible are visible to Him.

It shows God as one who sets order in His household. Elders are to be honoured, accusations are to be tested, and sin is to be dealt with in front of others so that fear of sin grows. These instructions are not bureaucracy. They reflect a God who cares for the reputation of His name among outsiders, 'denying the adversary occasion for slander,' verse 14, and who knows that disorder in the church is a gift to the enemy.

It shows God as concerned with bodies and health. The small aside about Timothy's stomach and the little wine is easy to overlook, but it tells us that the God who inspired this letter does not despise a minister's frequent ailments. He allows His servants medicine and care.

For worship, the chapter says that the care of the vulnerable and the honour of faithful leaders are not additional to worship but part of it. A congregation that sings well and neglects its widows has not understood the God it sings to.

crossReferences.note: God forbids the mistreatment of any widow or orphan. The Law makes the widow a special concern of the whole community, and the church in Ephesus inherits that duty. Paul's insistence on honoring true widows has its roots in this old command.

God is called a father of the fatherless and a defender of widows. The widow who puts her hope in God, as in 1 Timothy 5:5, is trusting in this very character. The church's care for widows is meant to be a visible echo of what God is like.

The law that an ox must not be muzzled as it treads out grain is quoted in 1 Timothy 5:18. Paul reads it as a principle: those who labour in the word may share in the fruit of their work. He argues the same way in 1 Corinthians 9:9 to 10.

Jesus tells the seventy-two to stay in one house, for the worker is worthy of his wages. The words match the second quotation in 1 Timothy 5:18, which shows that a teacher's support was grounded in the teaching of Jesus Himself.

A single witness is not enough to establish wrongdoing; two or three are required. Verse 19 of the letter applies the principle to elders. The rule protects leaders, who are exposed to criticism, from being brought down by one hostile voice.

Jesus rebukes those who used the Corban excuse to avoid supporting their parents, and He points to the commandment to honour father and mother. Paul's insistence that children repay their parents in 1 Timothy 5:4 and 5:8 is in the same line.

The first recorded church administration was about widows. The Hellenistic Jewish widows were overlooked in the daily distribution, and the apostles responded by appointing seven men. The story shows that fair care of widows was a mark of the church from its beginning.

Pure and undefiled religion before God is to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained from the world. James and Paul put care for the vulnerable at the centre of what faithfulness looks like.

Anna, a widow of great age, never left the temple but worshipped night and day, fasting and praying. She is a picture of the enrolled widow of 1 Timothy 5:5 and 5:9 to 10, whose life is given to prayer and whose faith is known.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders to keep watch over themselves and the flock and to shepherd the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood. The elders of 1 Timothy 5:17 serve a flock that has been bought at the highest price.
Elders are to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for greed but with eagerness. The text balances 1 Timothy 5:17. Leaders deserve honour and support, and they must not use the office for gain.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis on, the story keeps asking who will care for those the world forgets. In Eden the first human community was one of mutual help, Genesis 2:18. After the fall, the strong preyed on the weak, and the Law stepped in with provisions for the widow, the orphan and the stranger, which show what God's people were meant to be. Israel often failed, and the prophets cried out for justice for widows, Isaiah 1:17, the same cry that Paul echoes in the Ephesian church.

The chapter answers the problem of what a redeemed community looks like in practice. It is not a loose gathering of individuals but a household, with fathers and mothers and brothers and sisters, in which the vulnerable are known and the labourers are honoured. The church takes up Israel's calling and puts it into effect for a new people, as Acts 2:44 to 45 and 6:1 to 6 illustrate.

The passage also looks at how a community can be harmed from within. Idleness, gossip, favouritism and careless leadership are the problems Paul names, and each is a form of the old disorder that began when the first pair turned from God. The church is meant to be a place where that disorder is being undone: accusations tested, sin faced, good deeds received.

The judgment of verses 24 and 25 points ahead to the day when what is hidden is made known. Paul says that sins and good deeds that now go unnoticed will come to light, which fits the picture elsewhere that God will judge the secrets of men through Christ Jesus, Romans 2:16. In the new creation the household of God is complete: there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, no widow left alone, and God Himself dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The care practiced now is a rehearsal for that life.

quiz.q: How does Paul tell Timothy to relate to different members of the church?

options.text: As family: older men as fathers, younger women as sisters, and so on.
options.note: Verses 1 and 2 frame the church as a family to be treated with familial respect.

options.text: As employees under a strict manager.
options.note: The image is family, not a workplace hierarchy.

options.text: As strangers to keep at a distance.
options.note: Paul urges warm, familial treatment, not distance.

options.text: As rivals to be kept in check.
options.note: They are family to be honored, not rivals.

quiz.q: Who bears first responsibility for a widow with living family?

options.text: Her own children and grandchildren, as an act of godliness.
options.note: Verse 4 places the first duty on the family.

options.text: The state, with no role for the family.
options.note: Paul assigns the primary duty to relatives, not to outsiders.

options.text: The church alone, regardless of family.
options.note: The church helps the truly alone; families care for their own first.

options.text: No one; she must fend for herself.
options.note: Scripture insists she be cared for, first by family.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about someone who will not provide for his own household?

options.text: He has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
options.note: Verse 8 states this strong warning.

options.text: He has simply made an understandable choice.
options.note: Paul treats it as a grave denial of the faith, not a neutral choice.

options.text: He is more spiritual for trusting God to provide.
options.note: Neglect of family is condemned, not commended as faith.

options.text: It makes no difference to his standing.
options.note: Paul says it amounts to denying the faith.

quiz.q: What are elders who lead well worthy of?

options.text: Double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.
options.note: Verse 17 calls for double honor, including support.

options.text: Unquestioning obedience with no accountability.
options.note: They are honored, yet still subject to fair discipline, verses 19 and 20.

options.text: Suspicion and constant accusation.
options.note: Accusations require two or three witnesses; they are not to be entertained lightly.

options.text: Nothing beyond a bare thank-you.
options.note: Paul calls for double honor, including material provision.

quiz.q: How is Timothy to handle accusations and discipline among leaders?

options.text: Without bias or partiality, testing accusations by two or three witnesses.
options.note: Verses 19 to 21 require witnesses and impartiality.

options.text: By believing every accusation at once.
options.note: Accusations need witnesses; they are not to be entertained lightly.

options.text: By favoring his friends and allies.
options.note: He is charged to do nothing out of partiality.

options.text: By ignoring persistent sin to keep the peace.
options.note: Persistent sin is to be rebuked openly, verse 20.

questions: Paul treats the church as a family. Who in your congregation could you honor and care for more as a genuine father, mother, brother, or sister?
Caring for aging parents is called godliness pleasing to God. How are you carrying, or neglecting, that duty toward your own family right now?
The lonely widow put her hope in God and prayed night and day. What might her example teach you about turning need into prayer?
Elders who labor in the word deserve double honor. How well does your church honor and support those who preach and teach, and how do you play a part?
Timothy was charged to act without partiality. Where are you tempted to let friendship or bias shape a judgment that should be fair?

translationNotes.note: Older man renders presbyteros, the same word translated elder in verse 17; here it means an older man by age, not the church office.
Double honor translates a phrase carrying both esteem and material support, as the quotations in verse 18 confirm.
The two quotations are Deuteronomy 25:4 and Luke 10:7; Paul introduces both with the Scripture says, treating Jesus' words as Scripture.
